summary: AgroTwin helps Egyptian farmers choose their next crops, and see the water cost, before planting. Egypt has about 502 m³ of renewable water per person a year, half the water-poverty line, and farming uses most of it. A farmer taps their field on a map and describes the farm in Egyptian Arabic, by text or voice. AgroTwin replays each candidate rotation through 32 years of NASA POWER daily weather, adjusted to today's climate, and a daily FAO-56 soil-water model turns each run into yield, irrigation and profit, including price swings and canal shortfalls. The farmer gets a three-year plan with ranges for good, normal and bad years. Our trained Field Pulse model uses MODIS greenness and NASA weather to forecast each field 16 days ahead and flag fields that fall behind; on fields never seen in training, its error was 47% lower than assuming no change. Our VERDEX robot, an ESP32 rover with soil, air and rain sensors and a leaf camera, adds field detail that satellites miss and narrows the forecast range (robot data is simulated in this demo). At a Nile Delta test field, faba bean and maize beat wheat and rice in the model: 57% higher median profit and 27% less irrigation water. Next, we will test this against real harvests. Parts of the code and documentation were written with AI assistance and reviewed by the team.
details:
What it does and how it works

AgroTwin is a crop-planning tool that lets an Egyptian farmer try a crop rotation on past weather before planting it. The farmer taps their field on a map and describes the farm in Egyptian Arabic, by typing or speaking: what they grow, how much land they have, whether the soil is salty and whether canal water runs short. AgroTwin then replays every candidate rotation through 32 years of NASA POWER daily weather, with each past year warmed to match today's measured climate trend. A daily FAO-56 soil-water model treats the root zone like a water tank and turns each replay into crop stress, yield, irrigation need and profit, including price swings, canal shortfalls and soil salinity. The farmer gets a three-year plan with sowing dates, water use, and profit shown as a range for good, normal and bad years, plus a printable field card. During the season, our trained model Field Pulse forecasts each field's greenness 16 days ahead from MODIS data and NASA weather, and flags fields that fall behind. Our VERDEX field robot adds soil readings that narrow the season's forecast range.

Benefits

- Field-specific numbers before planting, instead of regional advice or habit.

- Honest uncertainty: every result is a range, and the bad-year outcome is always shown.

- Built for real farmers: Egyptian Arabic, voice, phone, and offline once a field is saved.

- Fast: a new plan is ready in about 2 seconds, so the farmer can ask "what if?" in conversation.

- Traceable: every number on screen is tagged with its source (NASA data, our calculation, the robot, a quoted price or a stated assumption).

Intended impact

Egypt has about 502 m³ of renewable water per person each year, half the water-poverty line, and farming uses about 79% of the country's water withdrawals, so each season's crop choice is also a water decision. At a Nile Delta test field, our replay found that switching from wheat and rice to faba bean and maize raised median profit by 57% and cut irrigation water by 27%. When five neighbouring farms planned together, the worst canal week dropped by 55%. These are model results, not measured harvests. We want extension officers and cooperatives to use AgroTwin to advise many farmers at once, starting with a supervised pilot that compares our plans with real harvests.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Backend: Python with FastAPI, NumPy and pandas.

- Field Pulse: scikit-learn gradient-boosted quantile trees with conformal calibration, trained on 482,744 samples.

- Frontend: JavaScript, HTML and CSS with Leaflet maps and Plotly charts; installable, works offline.

- NASA data: NASA POWER daily weather since 1981; MODIS MOD13Q1 greenness and MOD16 evapotranspiration from NASA GIBS and ORNL DAAC; SMAP and IMERG map layers; the NASA-IBM Prithvi foundation model, tested for future crop-type detection.

- Conversation: a rule engine handles plan changes; a language model (NVIDIA Nemotron) answers open questions using only numbers the engines computed.

- Hardware (VERDEX): ESP32 controller in C++ with FreeRTOS; servo-lowered soil-moisture probe, DHT22 air sensor, rain sensor and pan-tilt leaf camera; four-wheel chassis designed in SolidWorks; a 19.8 KB TensorFlow Lite model on the robot that flags faulty sensor readings; MQTT over Wi-Fi, a watchdog and a safety motor stop.

- Deployment: GitHub and Vercel. Code: https://github.com/Ali-M-Kotb/agrotwin

How it is creative

Most tools give one forecast. AgroTwin turns 32 years of NASA records into a set of possible futures for one specific field, so a farmer can see how a plan would have played out in a drought year or a heat wave. It combines satellites with a robot on the ground, whose readings sharpen the satellite-based forecast. It pairs physics with machine learning: removing the physics inputs from Field Pulse made its error 27% worse. And it hides all of this behind a conversation in Egyptian Arabic.

Factors our team considered

- Validity: tests on held-out seasons, independent fields and simple baselines; on fields never used in training, Field Pulse had 47% less error than assuming no change. We also report what did not work.

- Honesty: robot data is labelled as simulated, and results are never presented as measured harvests.

- Farmer reality: small plots (often under one feddan), low literacy, weak internet, canal schedules and government rules on rice area.

- Economics: quoted 2026 prices, and the farmer can edit every assumption.

- Water fairness: neighbours affect each other through shared canals.

- Cost: NASA data is free, and the app runs on one laptop or a free cloud tier.

- AI use: parts of the code and documentation were written with AI assistance and reviewed by the team.
